The Acoupa weakfish Cynoscion acoupa is a large, fast-growing sciaenid that supports important fisheries along the tropical Atlantic coast of South America. Its life history is characterized by a rapid early growth phase and a moderately long reproductive lifespan. Under the prevailing thermal regime of its native habitat, around 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active females was estimated at 3% [GSI = 3%]. The thermal conditions at this temperature also influence the species' maximum recorded longevity, which field studies estimate at approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years], a lifespan that is considerable for a fish reaching such large ultim at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]ate dimensions.

Sexual maturation in Cynoscion acoupa is closely tied to body size, occurring well before the attainment of maximum length. The total length at puberty, marking the onset of reproductive capability, has been measured at 42.7 cm [Lp = 42.7 cm], a point at which females have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to initiate vitellogenesis. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for females at this length is 723 g [Wwp = 723 g], a mass that indicates a significant energetic investment in somatic growth prior to the first spawning event. This size at maturity, which is relatively small compared to the species' ultimate attainable length, is a common life-history strategy among fast-growing sciaenids, allowing individuals to enter the reproductive population at a relatively young age while still having the potential for considerable further growth. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a standard allometric power function documented for the genus.

The early life stages of Cynoscion acoupa are characterized by a pelagic, dispersive larval phase, and the initial mass of the newly hatched individual is remarkably low. Based on the measured egg diameter of 0.72 mm, the wet weight at birth is calculated to be approximately 0.0002 g [Wwb = approximately 0.0002 g], a value that places the yolk-sac larva among the smallest of the large-bodied sciaenids. This initial mass is entirely supported by endogenous yolk reserves during the lecithotrophic stage, necessitating a rapid transition to first exogenous feeding before the point of no return is reached. The tiny size of the prolarva at eclosion reflects the classic teleost strategy of producing large numbers of small, pelagic eggs, which maximizes the probability of larval survival in a patchy planktonic environment but also subjects the earliest life stages to high rates of natural mortality.

As the fish progresses through the pelagic larval and juvenile phases, growth rates remain high, enabling individuals to reach a substantial body mass before the onset of reproductive senescence. The ultimate wet weight achieved by Cynoscion acoupa has been estimated at 13076 g [Wwi = 13076 g], a value derived from the length-weight relationship for the species and corresponding to the asymptotic length. This maximum recorded body mass represents a considerable investment in structural growth and lipid storage, allowing adults to sustain multiple spawning events across their long lives. Individuals nearing this size are typically apex predators within their estuarine and coastal habitats, feeding on fish and crustaceans. The capacity to reach such a large ultimate mass is a key factor in the species' commercial importance, as larger individuals yield higher market value and are preferentially targeted by both artisanal and industrial fisheries.

The size structure of the adult population is highly skewed toward the large body masses that confer a reproductive advantage, and the ultimate total length of 110 cm [Li = 110 cm] represents the largest individuals recorded in fishery-independent surveys. This length is consistent with the general pattern observed among large sciaenid species that inhabit turbid, productive coastal waters. The extreme size of these terminal adults is thought to be facilitated by the relatively moderate thermal regime of the species' range, with water temperatures averaging 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] supporting high metabolic rates and efficient food conversion throughout the active growing season. While the maximum recorded longevity of 23 years [am = 23 years] under these conditions is substantial, it is not exceptional among sciaenids of comparable body size, with some congeneric species exceeding 30 years in cooler, higher-latitude environments at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. The interplay between temperature-driven metabolic demands and the allocation of energy to somatic growth ultimately defines the upper boundary of size and age in this species.
